summary.text: The support of a real-valued function is the part of its domain whose elements are not mapped to zero.
When the domain is a topological space, the support is the smallest closed set containing all points not mapped to zero.
In probability, the support of a distribution can loosely be thought of as the closure of the set of possible values of a random variable with that distribution.

facts.label: Basic idea
facts.value: Elements of the domain not mapped to zero

facts.label: Compact support
facts.value: On the real line, it means the support is bounded

facts.label: Bump functions
facts.value: Real-valued smooth functions with compact support

facts.label: Essential support
facts.value: Depends on the measure and may be smaller

facts.label: Random variable
facts.value: Smallest closed set with probability one

items.prompt: A function is defined on the numbers 1 to 10 and equals zero everywhere except at 2, 5 and 7. Which set is its support?

options.label: The numbers 1 to 10
The numbers 2, 5 and 7
The numbers 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10
The number zero

items.explain: The support is the subset of the domain whose elements are not mapped to zero.

items.prompt: A function is nonzero at every point strictly between -1 and 1, and zero outside. Why is its support the closed interval including -1 and 1?

options.label: Because the function is nonzero at -1 and 1
Because a support always contains the ends of its domain
Because the support is the smallest closed set containing the nonzero points
Because the function has to be continuous

items.explain: The support is the smallest closed set containing all points not mapped to zero, so it is the closure of the open interval.

items.prompt: A function on the real line is nonzero only between -5 and 5, and zero everywhere else. Does it have compact support?

options.label: No: compact support means zero at every point
Yes: its support is closed and bounded, so it is compact
No: that needs a domain of separated values
Yes: but only if it is a smooth function

items.explain: On the real line a function has compact support exactly when its support is bounded, since a subset is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

items.prompt: A function never equals zero anywhere on the real line, though it fades toward zero far away. What is its support?

options.label: Only the point where it is largest
A closed interval around its peak
The empty set
The entire real line

items.explain: Since there is no point where the function is zero, its support is the entire set of real numbers, which is not compact.

items.prompt: A random variable can only ever take the values 1, 2 or 3. Loosely, what is the support of its distribution?

options.label: The set containing 1, 2 and 3
The whole interval from 1 to 3
The set containing 0, 1, 2 and 3
The entire real line

items.explain: The support can loosely be thought of as the closure of the set of possible values, here just 1, 2 and 3.

items.prompt: Beyond the function itself, what else does the essential support of a function depend on?

options.label: How many zeros the function has
The measure used on the domain
Whether the function is smooth
The function's value at the origin

items.explain: The essential support depends on the measure as well as on the function, and it may be strictly smaller than the closed support.
